content.title: Stellantis delays strategic plan amid uncertainty in US and EU
content.summary:
STORY: Stellantis is set to delay its strategic plan to the second quarter of next year. 

That’s to give CEO Antonio Filosa more time to address major uncertainties in its key markets…

Which includes rising trade barriers in the U.S. and evolving regulation in the European Union.

Filosa warned in July of a $1.73 billion hit from U.S. tariffs in 2025. 

Last year, over 40% of its vehicles sold in the U.S. were imports largely from Mexico and Canada… 

On which Washington has since imposed tariffs of 25%. 

Filosa said last month he did not yet see the U.S. tariff scenario as final.

Meanwhile in Europe, Filosa needs to wait for the outcome of the EU Commission's review of its 2035 zero-emission regulation.

That's due at the end of this year.

The CEO has pledged new vehicle launches to reconnect with customers as he aimed to get the automaker back on track after a difficult 2024.

Stellantis said it expects to make final decisions on these launches “relatively soon”. 

Shares in the automaker, which closed down 7.3% on Friday, rebounded on Monday.

content.title: Carmakers accused of cheating emissions tests in UK lawsuits
content.summary:
STORY: Lawyers accused some of the world's biggest carmakers of manipulating diesel emissions tests.

The claims were made at London's High Court Monday by the legal representatives of 1.6 million claimants at the start of a huge trial.

Owners of diesel vehicles made by certain brands between 2012 and 2017 allege the companies cheated emissions tests and are suing.

The accused include Mercedes-Benz, Ford, Nissan, Renault, and Stellantis-owned Peugeot and Citroen.

The manufacturers are accused of using unlawful "defeat devices" which detected when vehicles were being tested.

The devices allegedly ensured nitrogen oxide emissions were kept within legal limits under test conditions.

The claimants' lawyers argue the emissions were far higher when the cars were on the road, and in some cases up to 12 times test limits.

They said this caused harm to the environment and entitled consumers to compensation.

But the carmakers have called the claims fundamentally flawed.

They argue there are justified reasons why systems to control emissions are calibrated to work differently in certain conditions.

They also reject any similarity with 2015's 'Dieselgate' scandal, when Volkswagen admitted using defeat devices.

It cost the German auto giant billions of dollars.

The trial is due to conclude next year.

content.summary: Stellantis (STLA) released its consolidated shipment estimates. Consolidated shipments for the three months ending September 30, were an estimated 1.3M units, a 13% increase y-o-y.
